title: Batch fallback could steal any already-claimed job at any time, causing double-processing
description:
Discovered while narrating every Pilobol.us article, running local worker and
AWS Batch fallback side by side deliberately to test both paths. Confirmed
after the fact: at least one job (society-has-a-strangler-fig, hash
30188669) shows worker_type=batch and completed_at in its final record even
though the local worker's own log clearly showed Claimed 30188669 followed
by Completed 30188669 for that exact hash -- both workers did the real
work, and whichever's mark_done call landed last silently overwrote the
other's result.

Root cause in cdk/lambdas/router/handler.py, _claim_job's ConditionExpression:

  #status = :pending OR
  (#status = :claimed AND (claim_deadline < :now_epoch OR claim_deadline < :now_str)) OR
  (#status = :claimed AND :is_batch = :true_val)

:is_batch and :true_val are both literal Python values computed before the
call (worker_type == batch), not DynamoDB attribute references -- the third
clause reduces to status = claimed AND True for every single Batch claim
attempt, unconditionally. Batch could claim (steal) a job at literally any
moment after it was already claimed by anyone else, deadline or not. Since
the Step Functions fallback execution starts at job creation time (not
after the local claim window expires -- see the architecture doc) and only
waits internally before its first claim attempt, this race window exists
on every single job that a local worker ever picks up before Batch's own
internal wait elapses -- which is the normal, common case, not an edge
case.

Separately, the deadline check itself was also broken: claim_deadline is
written as a Decimal a few lines below and confirmed Decimal in every live
record checked directly via DynamoDB scan, but the condition compared it
against both a Decimal (:now_epoch) and a string (:now_str) in an OR --
comparing a Number attribute against a String literal with < is a type
mismatch. This didn't show up as a visible production error (real DynamoDB
apparently tolerates or short-circuits it in this OR context), but it broke
outright -- TypeError, not silently -- the moment a straightforward moto
based regression test exercised the same condition, which is what surfaced
it.

Fixed in cdk/lambdas/router/handler.py:
1. Removed the unconditional Batch-override clause entirely. The
   remaining two clauses (claim if pending, or reclaim if the existing
   claim has genuinely expired) are the correct, uniform mutex semantics
   for every claimant -- no special-casing needed once Batch is made to
   respect the same deadline everyone else does.
2. Removed the :now_str half of the deadline comparison; compare only
   against :now_epoch (Decimal), matching claim_deadline's actual stored
   type.

Added a regression test, test_batch_cannot_steal_an_unexpired_local_claim
in cdk/tests/test_router.py: creates a job, claims it as local, asserts a
subsequent Batch claim attempt on the same still-valid claim returns 409
and leaves worker_type/claimed_by unchanged. Full router suite passes
(17/17).

This needs an actual cdk deploy (Code.from_asset Lambda, not something that
ships via the Amplify site build) to reach the live function -- filing this
now, deploying separately right after.

comments.author: home
comments.text: Deployed and verified live: auritus deploy pushed the fixed RouterFn (only the Lambda code asset changed per cdk diff, confirmed before deploying). Live-fire test against production: created a job, claimed it as local (200, worker_type=local), then attempted to claim the same still-live job as batch -- correctly rejected with 409 already_claimed, worker_type stayed local. Test job released afterward.
